newsitem.title: UK: Labour to set control total before spending round.
newsitem.headline: Labour to set control total before spending round.

text.p: A Labour government would maintain present practice of setting a "control total" for non-cyclical public spending before opening detailed spending negotiations with individual ministries, Godon Brown, the party's economic spokesman, said on Monday.
Brown said the Treasury was right to plan ahead in step with the economic cycle by separating the cyclical element of public spending from the remainder.
"This will continue," he said in a speech setting out Labour's approach to public spending.
"I will also continue to set the new control total in advance of the spending round, since this approach contributes to prudence and stability," Brown said.
In the interests of both stable finances and effective budgeting, he said there could be no assumption that totals would be automatically adjusted upwards in the event of changes in inflation.

The onus would be on departments to spend their budgets efficiently. The Treasury would enhance its auditing processes, complemented by monitoring by the National Audit Office and the Audit Commission, Brown said.
The aim, Brown said, was to ensure that "we are wise spenders not big spenders".
He said New Labour rejected the party's old litmus test on spending -- that the overall level of spending was proof of its socialist commitment.

"While government still has and must have a clear responsibility to advance the public interest, we do not make the mistake of equating this with a commitment to inexorable increases in public spending," he said.
New Labour recognised that there was a public interest in ensuring the best opportunities but did not assume this meant more public ownership or more public spending in every area, he said.

"The only test is how the public interest is best served. There is no instinct towards more public spending. Instead there is an instinct -- and a commitment -- to ensure the public interest is advanced as effectively as possible," he added.
